'''Bertram Josef Richard Batlogg''' (born 1950) is an [[People of Austria|Austrian]] physicist known for his research on [[high-temperature superconductivity]].<ref name=aps-adler>{{cite web|title=2000 David Adler Lectureship Award in the Field of Materials Physics Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/units/dmp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Bertram&last_nm=Batlogg&year=2000|publisher=American Physical Society|accessdate=27 July 2012}}</ref>

Batlogg was born in the town of [[Bludenz]] in [[Austria]]. He is the great-grandson of the freedom fighter {{Ill|Johann Josef Batlogg|de|Johann Josef Batlogg|WD=}}.<ref name=loccata>{{cite web|title=The Physicist Bertram Batlogg|url=http://galileo.telesis.at/media-contents/litz-river-walkabout/p02-4-phsicst/|publisher=Loccata|accessdate=27 July 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160202232258/http://galileo.telesis.at/media-contents/litz-river-walkabout/p02-4-phsicst/|archivedate=2 February 2016}}</ref> Batlogg was educated in the Swiss Federal Institute [[ETH Zurich]], earning his diploma in physics in 1974, and his [[Ph.D.]] in 1979 working with mixed valence [[rare-earth element|rare-earth compounds]].<ref name=eth-profile>{{cite web|title=Prof. Dr. Bertram Batlogg|url=https://www.bi.id.ethz.ch/personensuche/detail.do?lang=EN&pid=17B3D|publisher=ETH Zurich|accessdate=27 July 2012}}</ref> He then joined [[Bell Labs]], first as a post-doctoral researcher, and rising to be the head of the Solid State Physics and Materials Research Division at Bell Labs by 1986.<ref name=lucent-profile>{{cite web|title=He Turned Up The Heat On a Very Cold Subject|url=http://www.bell-labs.com/user/feature/archives/batlogg/|work=Bell Labs|publisher=Alcatel-Lucent|accessdate=27 July 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/19990202103416/http://www.bell-labs.com/user/feature/archives/batlogg/|archivedate=2 February 1999}}</ref> After the discovery of [[high-temperature superconductors]] in 1987, Batlogg studied various [[cuprate|cuprate compounds]] and together with [[Robert Cava]] discovered several transition metal oxide superconductors with high transition temperatures.<ref name=lucent-profile /> In 1997, they won the Bernd Matthias Prize for their research on superconductivity.

Starting in 1998, Batlogg worked with Christian Kloc and [[Schön scandal|Jan Hendrik Schön]] to study [[organic electronics|electronic properties of organic crystals]]. Over the next two years, the collaboration produced a series of ground-breaking papers regarding the properties of these materials. However, the experimental data provided by Schön were later shown to be fraudulent and several of the most important papers were retracted by the authors. The incident came to be known as the [[Schön scandal]]. Batlogg, Kloc and Schön's other collaborators were cleared in Sept 2002 of all scientific misconduct by an external committee appointed by Bell Labs.<ref name=science-service>{{cite journal|last=Service|first=Robert F.|title=Pioneering Physics Papers Under Suspicion for Data Manipulation|journal=Science|date=May 2002|volume=296|issue=5572|doi=10.1126/science.296.5572.1376|url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.296.5572.1376|accessdate=27 July 2012|pages=1376–1377|pmid=12029100|s2cid=35235316|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
<ref name="BeasleyReport">{{cite web|url=https://media-bell-labs-com.s3.amazonaws.com/pages/20170403_1709/misconduct-revew-report-lucent.pdf|title=Report of the Investigation Committee on the possibility of Scientific Misconduct in the work of Hendrik Schon and Coauthors|last1= Beasley |first1= Malcolm R.|date=September 2002|publisher=Bell Labs|first2= Supriyo |last2= Datta |first3= Herwig |last3= Kogelnik|first4= Herbert |last4= Kroemer |first5= Don|last5= Monroe}}</ref>
However, the committee questioned whether Batlogg met his professional responsibility to take "a sufficiently critical
stance with regard to the research in question". This question was left unanswered by the committee. In Oct 2002 and after, [[Science (journal)|''Science'']], ''[[Physical Review]]'', and ''[[Applied Physics Letters]]'' withdrew more than a dozen papers.

Batlogg joined ETH Zurich as a professor in 2000, where he remained until his retirement in 2016.<ref name=eth-profile /> The main research topics at ETH included superconductivity, physics of strongly correlated electrons and charge transport and trapping in molecular organic semiconductors. In the list of Most Cited Physicists published by the Institute for Scientific Information (ISI), covering 1981-June 1997, he is placed 4th with some 14000 citations. As of 2020, the Web of Science lists about 34000 citations and an [[h-index]] of 90+.
